y-m-18-01.title: Two groups with the same average: are their records similar too?
y-m-18-01.topic: Meaning and limits of the average
y-m-18-01.goal: Show with number examples you make yourself that individual records can differ greatly even when the average is the same, and say what cannot be known from the average alone.
y-m-18-01.material:
In 6th-grade PE class, two groups (5 students each) did sit-ups for 1 minute. The records are natural numbers of 0 or more (times).
Group A's records: 8 times, 9 times, 10 times, 11 times, 12 times.
For Group B, it is only known that the average of the 5 students' records is 10 times. The teacher said, “The two groups have the same average of 10 times, so they are equally good groups.”
y-m-18-01.thinking.0: Telling apart what one average can tell and what it cannot
y-m-18-01.thinking.1: Making data that satisfy the conditions yourself (a counterexample)
y-m-18-01.thinking.2: Saying what else needs to be checked besides the average
y-m-18-01.prereq.0: Knowing the meaning of the average (the value that evens out the data, 5th-grade level)
y-m-18-01.prereq.1: Addition and multiplication of natural numbers
y-m-18-01.s.s1.prompt: For Group B, it is only known that the average is 10 times. Choose all the statements about B that must be true.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write down two or three sets of records for 5 students with an average of 10 times yourself.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.hint.1: For each statement, test one by one whether you can make a set of records that does not fit it.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.o.a: The total of the 5 students' records is 50 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.r.a: This uses the relation that the total of the records is fixed by the average and the number of people.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.o.b: All 5 students did 8 or more, and no student did fewer than that.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.r.b: Even with an average of 10 times, one student can have a very low record such as 2. You may have taken the average as ‘the picture of every student.’
y-m-18-01.s.s1.o.c: If a student did fewer than 10 times, there is also a student who did more.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.r.c: You saw that the average is a balance point where the side below 10 times and the side above 10 times make up for each other.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.o.d: Among the 5 students, at least one student did exactly 10 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.r.d: The average can be a value nobody actually did. Even if the total is 50, as in 8, 9, 11, 11, 11 times, no student may have done 10 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.explain: The total of the records of 5 students with an average of 10 times must be 50 times, and if a student did fewer than 10 times, there must be a student who did more than 10 times to make up that shortfall. But you can't say that all did 8 or more or that some student surely did 10 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different sets of records for Group B with an average of 10 times in which the records of the student who did the most and the student who did the least differ by 12 times or more. (The 5 students' records a, b, c, d, e. Records that only change the order of people count as the same record.)
y-m-18-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write what you can know about all 5 students' records from the fact that the average is 10 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one student who did very few, and think about who could make up that shortfall.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.hint.2: Subtract the largest and smallest values of the records you made yourself and check that the difference is 12 or more.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.ok.c1: All the records are 0 or more.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The records must be 0 or more.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.ok.c2: All the records are natural numbers (times).
y-m-18-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The records are counts, so they must be natural numbers.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The average of the 5 students is not 10 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.ok.c4: The largest and smallest records differ by 12 times or more.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.fail.c4: The difference between the student who did the most and the student who did the least is less than 12 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.explain: For example, 2, 4, 10, 16, and 18 times have an average of 10 times, but the largest and smallest records differ by as much as 16 times. Even with the same average, a group whose records are close together (A) and a group whose records are spread out look different.
y-m-18-01.s.s3.prompt: What do you think about the teacher's statement, “The averages are the same, so the two groups are equally good”? Write it by comparing with the records you made above or with Group A, and also write one thing you would like to know besides the average.
y-m-18-01.s.s3.hint.0: Copy one line of the records you made above as it is and place it side by side with A.
y-m-18-01.s.s3.hint.1: Start with a sentence that fills in the blank of ‘The average is the same, but ___ is different.’
y-m-18-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. The average is the same, but ...
y-m-18-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the number example I gave, is it clear how the pictures of the records differ even though the average is the same?
y-m-18-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write specifically what you want to check besides the average (the lowest record, the highest record, the difference in records, etc.)?
y-m-18-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write a reason instead of just writing ‘different’?
y-m-18-01.s.s3.model.0: It's hard to agree. A is gathered at 8 to 12 times, but the 2, 4, 10, 16, and 18 times I made have a big difference from 2 to 18 times. Even with the same average, how spread out the records are is different, so I'd also like to know the highest and lowest records.
y-m-18-01.s.s3.model.1: By the average alone they are the same, but in the B I made, one student had only 2 and one had 18, so the difference in ability is big. It's hard to say everyone does equally well. I'd like to see each student's record.

y-m-18-02.title: When you toss two coins, which result comes up more often?
y-m-18-02.topic: Chance: working things out by splitting into cases
y-m-18-02.goal: Compare two explanations (all three results are the same / look at the coins separately and split into cases) with experiment data, revise your judgment, and say why we split into cases.
y-m-18-02.material:
You toss a red coin and a blue coin at the same time. Each coin has the same chance of heads and tails, and one coin does not affect the other.
Jia: “There are three results: [both heads], [one head and one tail], and [both tails], so they all have the same chance.”
Minho: “There are two coins, so we have to look at how each coin comes out separately.”
y-m-18-02.thinking.0: Comparing two explanatory models with data
y-m-18-02.thinking.1: Revising judgment and confidence after seeing data
y-m-18-02.thinking.2: Explaining why we count the cases separately
y-m-18-02.prereq.0: Saying chance as ‘the same / higher / lower’ (3rd–5th grade level)
y-m-18-02.s.s1.prompt: When two coins are tossed, which of the following do you think will come up most often? Choose the thought you have now.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write what side the blue coin can show when the red coin is heads.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write it the same way when the red coin is tails, and count how many ways there are in all.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.r.a: Think about whether there is a reason ‘both heads’ would come up especially often. Each coin has the same chance of heads.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.o.b: All three results come up about the same number of times
y-m-18-02.s.s1.r.b: This is the explanation that takes the results split into three kinds to have the same chance. It has not yet checked whether the number of ways each result can happen is the same.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.r.c: You are looking at whether there are more ways to make that result. You can test what the evidence is in the next step.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.o.d: You can't say anything before tossing them
y-m-18-02.s.s1.r.d: Tossing them is a good way too, but you can also work it out ahead of time by using the fact that there are two coins.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.explain: At this step it is a first guess. The guess that ‘the three results are the same’ is common too, but we will test it with data and working out cases in the next steps.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.acc.0: It is natural as a first guess. But whether the ‘three results’ have the same chance has to be tested, so let's check the data in the next step.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.prompt: This is a record of tossing two coins 40 times. Both heads 9 times, one head and one tail 21 times, and both tails 10 times. How do you judge Jia's explanation from this record?
y-m-18-02.s.s2.hint.0: If Jia's explanation is right, guess about how many times each of the three results should come up by dividing 40.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put it side by side with the actual records of 9, 21, and 10 and compare which result differs by how much.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.o.a: The explanation that the three results are the same is right, and 21 times just happened to come up a lot.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.r.a: You are putting the data down to chance. If the three results were the same, it would be natural for each to come up about 13 times out of 40; how common would it be to get 21?
y-m-18-02.s.s2.o.b: The coins are not fair, so one head and one tail came up a lot.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.r.b: The conditions said each coin has the same chance of heads and tails. Before blaming the coins, first look at how the results are counted.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.o.c: 40 is small, so no judgment can be made from this record.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.r.c: It is true the number of tosses is small, but the difference between 21 and 9 is quite big. Even if you can't be certain, you can compare whether the explanation fits the data.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.o.d: ‘One of each’ came up about twice as often as the others, so Jia's explanation is doubtful.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.r.d: You compared whether the explanation fits the data by looking at the ratio of the counts (9:21:10). 40 tosses is not a large number, so it is suitable to say ‘doubtful.’
y-m-18-02.s.s2.explain: If the three results were the same, as in Jia's explanation, each should come up about 13 times out of 40, but ‘one of each’ came up 21 times, about twice the others. 40 tosses is not many so we can't be certain, but Jia's explanation does not fit the data well.
y-m-18-02.s.s3.prompt: Now explain it so Jia understands. List the possible results by telling the two coins apart, and write why ‘one head and one tail’ comes up more often than ‘both heads.’
y-m-18-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write it like drawing a table, splitting into when the red coin is heads and when it is tails.
y-m-18-02.s.s3.hint.1: Among the cases you wrote, mark the ones that count as ‘one of each.’
y-m-18-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If we tell the red coin and the blue coin apart ...
y-m-18-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write all the possible cases without omission, telling the red coin and the blue coin apart?
y-m-18-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write clearly how many cases make ‘one head and one tail’?
y-m-18-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you point out where Jia's ‘there are three, so they're the same’ goes off?
y-m-18-02.s.s3.model.0: If we tell the red coin and the blue coin apart, there are 4 cases: (heads, heads), (heads, tails), (tails, heads), (tails, tails). Of these, ‘one of each’ is the two cases (heads, tails) and (tails, heads), so it comes up twice as often as ‘both heads.’
y-m-18-02.s.s3.model.1: The two coins are different, so (red heads, blue tails) and (red tails, blue heads) are different cases. Two of the 4 cases are one of each, so the chance is 1/2, and both heads is 1/4.

y-m-18-03.title: Haeun's band graph solution: what looks odd?
y-m-18-03.topic: Showing data with a band graph and checking it
y-m-18-03.goal: In a percentage-calculation solution, find the wrong line and the clue that ‘if the sum is not 100%, it is wrong,’ and make survey numbers that give the same band graph.
y-m-18-03.material: Haeun, a 6th grader, had the 40 students in her class each choose one ‘favorite season.’ The results are spring 12 students, summer 14 students, fall 8 students, and winter 6 students. Haeun solved as below to show it in a band graph. The whole band of a band graph is 100%.
y-m-18-03.thinking.0: Finding where the error in a solution is
y-m-18-03.thinking.1: Checking by yourself using the condition that the whole is 100%
y-m-18-03.thinking.2: Confirming that several survey sizes can make the same band graph
y-m-18-03.prereq.1: Meaning that the whole band of a band graph is 100%
y-m-18-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one wrong line in Haeun's solution. (Line numbers are counted from 1.)
y-m-18-03.s.s1.hint.0: Check each line by converting the percentage back to a number of people (e.g. how many of 40 students is 30%).
y-m-18-03.s.s1.hint.1: Look at whether the result of the last line fits the condition of a band graph.
y-m-18-03.s.s1.line.5: Adding all the percentages gives 30+35+2+15=82%. Even so, you can just fill and draw the band only up to 82%.
y-m-18-03.s.s1.explain: In line 4, 0.2 is 20%, but it was written as 2%. And in line 6, the sign that the sum is 82% and not 100% was seen but the graph was drawn anyway. The whole of a band graph is 100%, so if the percentages do not add up to 100, some line is wrong.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.prompt: The band graph of a survey in another class says ‘dodgeball 40%, soccer 30%, jump rope 20%, other 10%.’ Make 2 different versions of the number of people surveyed N (students) and the number in each item that could give this band graph. (N is a natural number of 60 or less.)
y-m-18-03.s.s2.hint.0: The other is 10%, so first write how many students each item is if the whole is 10 students.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.hint.1: Changing the total number of people, check whether each item comes out as a natural number of students.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.hint.2: Check whether the numbers of people you made match the total number of students and whether the percentages are unchanged.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The total number of students is a natural number from 1 to 60.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The total number of students must be a natural number of 60 or less.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.ok.c2: Each number of people is a natural number of 0 or more.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Each number of people must be a natural number of 0 or more.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The numbers of people in all the items add up to the total number of students.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of the numbers of people in the items differs from the total number of students.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.ok.c4: Dodgeball 40%, soccer 30%, and jump rope 20% are right.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The percentages of dodgeball, soccer, and jump rope are not 40%, 30%, and 20%.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.explain: If N=10, it is 4, 3, 2, 1 students, and if N=20, it is 8, 6, 4, 2 students. In both cases the percentages in the band graph are the same. 40%, 30%, 20%, and 10% can all be shown as natural numbers of people when N is a multiple of 10.
y-m-18-03.s.s3.prompt: So that Haeun doesn't make the same mistake again, tell her one way to find out for herself what is wrong before drawing a band graph.
y-m-18-03.s.s3.hint.0: Think about what percentage the whole band graph is, and how you could compare the calculated values with it.
y-m-18-03.s.s3.hint.1: Read the last line of Haeun's solution and think about what you should have noticed in that line.
y-m-18-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear ‘what is being checked’ (e.g. whether the sum is 100%)?
y-m-18-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you also write what to do when the result of the check is not 100?
y-m-18-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is it a specific method that Haeun can follow right away?
y-m-18-03.s.s3.model.0: Add up all the percentages and check whether they make 100%. If it's not 100, like 82%, something is wrong somewhere, so look at the lines you calculated again.
y-m-18-03.s.s3.model.1: If you check both that the numbers of people for each season add up to 40 and that the percentages add up to 100%, it's easy to find the wrong line.

y-m-18-04.title: If one bar is twice as tall, are the sales twice as much too?
y-m-18-04.topic: Scale and comparison in a bar graph
y-m-18-04.goal: Know that in a bar graph whose scale does not start at 0, the ratio of bar heights and the ratio of values can differ, and suggest ways to prevent misunderstanding.
y-m-18-04.material: The number of books sold this month at neighborhood bookstores A and B is shown in a bar graph. The vertical scale has 80 books at the very bottom and then 85, 90, 95, and 100 books going up (it does not start from 0 books). A bar's height is measured from the bottom mark (80 books) to the end of the bar. The end of A's bar is at 90 books and the end of B's bar is at 100 books. So B's bar looks about twice as tall as A's bar.
y-m-18-04.thinking.0: Telling the impression a graph gives from the real values
y-m-18-04.thinking.1: Examining how the starting point of the scale affects comparison
y-m-18-04.thinking.2: Making pairs of values that satisfy conditions and suggesting improvements
y-m-18-04.prereq.0: Reading the scale of a bar graph (4th-grade level)
y-m-18-04.prereq.1: Comparing two numbers by multiplication (how many times)
y-m-18-04.s.s1.prompt: Three friends looked at this graph and spoke. Choose all the statements that are right.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.hint.0: Check directly with the sales numbers written on the scale whether Jisu's statement is right.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.hint.1: Look at how many books the bottom of the vertical scale is, and from where the bar heights are measured.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.o.a: Jisu: “B's bar is twice as tall, so we can say the sales are exactly twice as much.”
y-m-18-04.s.s1.r.a: You read the bar height as the sales themselves. Check the scale for where the bar height is measured from.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.o.b: Doyun: “If you read the scale, A is 90 books and B is 100 books. It's not twice.”
y-m-18-04.s.s1.r.b: You checked by reading the values from the scale instead of the impression of the graph.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.o.c: Raon: “The scale starts at 80 books, so the ratio of the bar heights and the ratio of the sales are different.”
y-m-18-04.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out that the starting point of the scale affects the comparison.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.o.d: Seoeun: “The graph itself is wrong, so this data can't be used and has to be surveyed again.”
y-m-18-04.s.s1.r.d: The values in the graph are not wrong. It is easy to misunderstand depending on how you read it, but the data is not wrong.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.explain: The bar heights are measured from 80 books, so A is drawn 10 books high and B is drawn 20 books high, and it looks like twice. But the real sales, 90 books and 100 books, are not twice. The graph itself is not wrong; it is easy to misunderstand because of the starting point of the scale.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.prompt: In a graph like this, whose scale starts at 80 books, make 2 different pairs of sales in which B's bar is drawn exactly twice as tall as A's bar but B's real sales are 1.2 times A's or less. (A and B are natural numbers of books greater than 80.)
y-m-18-04.s.s2.hint.0: Use the fact that a bar height is measured by how much more than 80 books it is.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.hint.1: Choose A, and work out how many books B must be for B's bar height to be twice A's.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.hint.2: With the values you chose, check yourself about how many times A's sales B's sales are.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.ok.c1: A is more than 80 books and both are natural numbers.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.fail.c1: A must be greater than 80 and both must be natural numbers.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.ok.c2: B's bar height, measured from the 80 books mark, is twice A's bar.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.fail.c2: B's bar height, measured from the 80 books mark, is not twice A's bar height.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.ok.c3: B's sales are 1.2 times A's or less.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.fail.c3: B's sales are more than 1.2 times A's.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.explain: For example, if (A, B)=(85, 90), the bar heights are 5 books and 10 books, which is twice, but the real sales are about 1.06 times. For (90, 100) it is about 1.11 times. If the scale does not start from 0, a small difference can look big.
y-m-18-04.s.s3.prompt: If you print this graph in the bookstore's newsletter, how could you change or add to it so that readers do not misunderstand that ‘B sold twice as much’? Suggest at least one way.
y-m-18-04.s.s3.hint.0: Think about whose method, Doyun's or Raon's above, would help the reader.
y-m-18-04.s.s3.hint.1: Think about where someone seeing the graph for the first time could look to find the values.
y-m-18-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If we ... the ... of the graph, then ...
y-m-18-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the method you suggested really reduce the problem of ‘looking like twice’?
y-m-18-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you let readers find out the values directly?
y-m-18-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Compared with other methods, can you name one good point of your suggestion?
y-m-18-04.s.s3.model.0: It would be good to draw the vertical scale starting from 0 books so that the bar heights look in line with the real size of the sales.
y-m-18-04.s.s3.model.1: If you write the values like 90 books and 100 books above the bars and mark that the scale starts at 80 books, readers will misunderstand less.

y-m-18-05.title: If we combine the two classes, what is the overall average?
y-m-18-05.topic: Interpreting the average of several groups combined
y-m-18-05.goal: Know that the overall average cannot be fixed from the averages of two groups alone, say what other information is needed, and make numbers of students that fit the conditions yourself.
y-m-18-05.material: Class 1 and Class 2 in 6th grade took the same math assessment. All the scores are from 0 to 100 points. Class 1's average is 70 points and Class 2's average is 80 points. Hajun said, “The average of all the students in the two classes combined is (70+80)÷2=75 points.” The numbers of students in the two classes have not been told yet.
y-m-18-05.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-18-05.thinking.1: Reasoning about which way the size of a group moves the average
y-m-18-05.thinking.2: Making combinations of numbers of people that fit the conditions
y-m-18-05.prereq.0: Knowing the meaning of the average (5th-grade level)
y-m-18-05.prereq.1: Multiplication and addition of natural numbers
y-m-18-05.s.s1.prompt: For Hajun's 75 points to be exactly right, which of the following would have to be known?
y-m-18-05.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine whether the overall average would be near 75 points if Class 1 has 1 student and Class 2 has 99 students.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, test one by one which way the overall average moves if it is true.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.o.a: Class 1 has more students than Class 2.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.r.a: The overall average gets closer to the average of the side with more students. Then think about whether it would be 75 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.o.b: The two classes have the same number of students.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.r.b: This considered that the size of a group affects the average. If the sizes are equal, the two averages count equally.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.o.c: Both classes have a student who scored 100 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.r.c: Even if the top score is the same, the overall average does not become the middle of the two averages.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.o.d: All the students in Class 2 scored 80 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.r.d: Even if all the scores in Class 2 are the same, if the numbers of students in the two classes differ, the overall average differs.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.explain: Only when the two classes have the same number of students is the overall average 75 points, exactly the middle of the two averages. If the numbers of students differ, the overall average moves toward the class with more students.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.prompt: Now you know that Class 1 has 20 students and Class 2 has 30 students. How does the overall average compare with 75 points?
y-m-18-05.s.s2.hint.0: Think about which of the 20-student class and the 30-student class has more influence on the whole with its scores.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.hint.1: Draw like a number line where between 70 and 80 points the overall average would be closer.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.o.a: It is the same as 75 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.r.a: You mixed the averages of two classes with different numbers of students in equal amounts.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.r.b: The class with more students is the one with higher scores, but you thought in the direction of the overall average going down.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.o.c: You can't tell whether it is higher or lower than 75 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.r.c: You know both classes' numbers of students and averages, so you can fix the direction.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.r.d: You judged that the overall average moves toward the 80-point average of Class 2, which has more students.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.explain: Class 2 has more students and Class 2's average is higher, so the overall average is higher than 75 points. In fact, (70×20+80×30)÷50=76 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.prompt: Class 1's average of 70 points and Class 2's average of 80 points stay the same. Make 2 different versions of the numbers of students so that the combined overall average of the two classes is exactly 78 points. (Class 1 has m students, Class 2 has n students, each class has 5 or more, and the two classes together have 50 or fewer.)
y-m-18-05.s.s3.hint.0: If the overall average is 78 points, think about which it is closer to, the 70-point class or the 80-point class.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how far 78 is from 70 and how far from 80, between 70 and 80.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.hint.2: With the numbers of students you chose, check yourself that the overall average really is 78 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.ok.c1: Each class has a natural number of 5 or more students.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.fail.c1: The number of students in each class must be a natural number of 5 or more.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.ok.c2: The two classes together have 50 or fewer.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.fail.c2: The two classes together have more than 50.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.fail.c3: The overall average is not 78 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.explain: For example, with 5 students in Class 1 and 20 in Class 2, the sum of the scores is 70×5+80×20=1950, and dividing by 25 students gives 78 points. When Class 2 has 4 times as many students as Class 1, the overall average is 78 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.prompt: Write why, when Class 1 has 5 students and Class 2 has 20, the overall average is 78 points and not 75 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.hint.0: Compare which class's score 75 points and 78 points are closer to.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.hint.1: First write how the numbers of students in the two classes differ and then continue with the reason.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write that the class with more students has a bigger effect on the overall average?
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Do the direction of going higher than 75 points and the reason agree?
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.model.0: Class 2 has 4 times as many students as Class 1, so the average gets closer to Class 2's score of 80 points. That's why it is 78 points and not 75 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.model.1: It is because the score of the class with more students has a bigger effect on the overall average. Class 2 has 4 times as many, so the overall average is pulled toward 80 points.

y-m-18-06.title: Let's make a spinner that favors no one
y-m-18-06.topic: Expressing chance with numbers: a fair spinner
y-m-18-06.goal: Judge that chances are the same by the number of sections, design several spinners that satisfy the conditions, and say that ‘fairness’ and ‘how often there is a winner’ are different matters.
y-m-18-06.material: Haeun and Doyun play a spinner game. The spinner is divided evenly into 12 sections of the same size, and the arrow is equally likely to stop on any section. Each section has one of ‘Haeun,’ ‘Doyun,’ or ‘blank’ written on it. The person whose name is on the section where the arrow stops gets 1 point, and if it is ‘blank,’ nobody gets a point. ‘Fair’ means that the two people have the same chance of getting a point.
y-m-18-06.thinking.0: Comparing equal chances by the number of sections
y-m-18-06.thinking.2: Telling fairness apart from another property (how often there is a winner)
y-m-18-06.prereq.0: Meaning and size comparison of the fractions 1/2, 1/4, 1/3
y-m-18-06.prereq.1: Saying chance as ‘the same / higher / lower’
y-m-18-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the fair spinners among the following. (All have 12 sections.)
y-m-18-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each spinner, write side by side Haeun's and Doyun's chances of getting a point as the number of sections out of 12.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.hint.1: Leave out the blank sections and compare only the two people's numbers of sections.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.o.a: Haeun 6 sections, Doyun 3 sections, blank 3 sections
y-m-18-06.s.s1.r.a: One person's number of sections is double the other's. Look at how the number of sections fixes the size of the chance.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.o.b: Haeun 5 sections, Doyun 5 sections, blank 2 sections
y-m-18-06.s.s1.r.b: You judged fairness by comparing the two people's numbers of sections, not the number of blank sections.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.o.c: Haeun 5 sections, Doyun 4 sections, blank 3 sections
y-m-18-06.s.s1.r.c: 5 sections and 4 sections look similar, but the chances are not the same.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.o.d: Haeun 4 sections, Doyun 4 sections, blank 4 sections
y-m-18-06.s.s1.r.d: Even with many blanks, it is fair if the two people's numbers of sections are the same.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.explain: To be fair, Haeun and Doyun must have the same number of sections. How many blank sections there are has nothing to do with fairness. With Haeun 6 sections and Doyun 3 sections, Haeun's chance of getting a point (1/2) is double Doyun's (1/4), and with 5 sections and 4 sections it differs as 5/12 and 4/12.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.prompt: You are making a new 12-section spinner. Make 2 different spinners that are fair (Haeun's number of sections h and Doyun's number of sections d are equal) and in which the chance of ‘blank’ is from 1/6 to 1/2. (The number of blank sections is k. h, d, and k are natural numbers and add up to 12 sections.)
y-m-18-06.s.s2.hint.0: First think about how to split the Haeun sections and Doyun sections so that it is fair.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.hint.1: Write how many of the 12 sections is a chance of 1/6 for blank and how many is 1/2, and fix the range.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.hint.2: Choose Haeun's number of sections, work out what happens to the remaining sections, and check that it fits the conditions.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.ok.c1: All the numbers of sections are natural numbers of 1 or more.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.fail.c1: All three numbers of sections must be natural numbers of 1 or more.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The numbers of sections do not add up to 12.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.ok.c3: Haeun's and Doyun's numbers of sections are equal, so it is fair.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.fail.c3: Haeun's and Doyun's numbers of sections differ, so it is not fair.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.ok.c4: The chance of blank is from 1/6 to 1/2.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.fail.c4: The chance of blank is not from 1/6 to 1/2.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.explain: (5, 5, 2), (4, 4, 4), and (3, 3, 6) are possible. If Haeun's and Doyun's numbers of sections are equal, the rest are blank, so the number of blank sections is 12 minus 2h, an even number, and the condition is met only when k is 2, 4, or 6.
y-m-18-06.s.s3.prompt: The spinner with (Haeun 3 sections, Doyun 3 sections, blank 6 sections) and the spinner with (Haeun 5 sections, Doyun 5 sections, blank 2 sections) are both fair. Write what would be different when you play the game with the two spinners.
y-m-18-06.s.s3.hint.0: Compare how many of the 12 sections are sections where nobody gets a point on the two spinners.
y-m-18-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write Haeun's chance of getting a point on each of the two spinners.
y-m-18-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write how the frequency of points in a round differs when there are many blanks and when there are few?
y-m-18-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state the difference while keeping that both spinners are fair?
y-m-18-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you state the chance with numbers like how many of the 12 sections?
y-m-18-06.s.s3.model.0: Both are fair because Haeun and Doyun have the same chance of winning. But (5, 5, 2) has only 2 blank sections, so nearly every time one of them gets a point, and (3, 3, 6) has half blanks, so there are many rounds where nobody gets a point.
y-m-18-06.s.s3.model.1: The more blank sections, the more likely a round gives no points. The spinner with 3 sections each has blank at 6/12, so one time in two nobody wins, but it is just as fair.

y-m-18-07.title: If we ask at the soccer field, is the result what the whole school thinks?
y-m-18-07.topic: Ways of collecting data and representativeness
y-m-18-07.goal: Know that results can change depending on how you choose the people to survey, and design for yourself a survey method that better represents the whole school.
y-m-18-07.material: Minseo, a 6th grader, wants to find out the activity that all 240 students in the school most want to do during break time. Minseo asked 30 students who were gathered at the soccer field during break, and 24 of them (80%) answered ‘soccer.’ Minseo plans to announce, “80% of the students at our school most want to play soccer!”
y-m-18-07.thinking.0: Criticizing the survey method that the result is based on
y-m-18-07.thinking.1: Revising your degree of confidence after seeing new data
y-m-18-07.prereq.1: Organizing survey results in a table (3rd–4th grade level)
y-m-18-07.s.s1.prompt: What do you think about Minseo's announcement sentence?
y-m-18-07.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine what kind of students would be gathered at the soccer field.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the result would change if the same question were asked in the library or in a classroom.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.o.a: She only asked at the soccer field, so it is hard to say it is the whole school's thinking.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.r.a: You pointed out that the way of choosing who to survey can affect the result.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.o.b: 30 students is a large enough number of people, so it can be announced as it is.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.r.b: You judged only by the number of people. Also look at where and whom she asked.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.o.c: 30 students is too few, so no survey can be trusted.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.r.c: The number of people matters too, but whom you ask comes first. Even a small number can be a clue if chosen evenly.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.o.d: It is as high as 80%, so it is fine to say ‘most.’
y-m-18-07.s.s1.r.d: You judged only by the high percentage. Look at what kind of people that percentage came from.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.explain: More students who want to play soccer may be gathered at the soccer field. So this result can tell what 'the students gathered at the soccer field' think, but it is hard to say it is what the whole school thinks.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.prompt: Minseo changed the method and drew 36 students by lottery of attendance numbers from the list of all students, so that grades and classes were evenly mixed, and asked them. 9 students (25%) answered ‘soccer.’ How do you judge now?
y-m-18-07.s.s2.hint.0: Compare how ‘whom was asked’ differs between the two surveys.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.hint.1: Imagine whether exactly 9 students would say ‘soccer’ if 36 students were drawn again.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.o.a: The 80% of the first 30 students is right, and the 25% of the 36 students this time is wrong.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.r.a: You said one result is surely right and threw away the other. Look at how the methods of the two surveys differ.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.o.b: Announce 52.5%, the exact middle of the two results, as the whole school's percentage.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.r.b: You just mixed two sets of data collected by different methods. Because the way of choosing whom to survey is different, mixing them may have no meaning.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.o.c: The 36 students' result is closer to the whole school, but we don't know the exact value.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.r.c: You decided how much to trust it based on the survey method, and also saw the limit that the 36 students are not the whole school either.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.o.d: 36 students is more than 30, so announce it as 25% of the whole school.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.r.d: You asserted it is exactly the same, based on the number of people. If different people are drawn, the result can be a little different too.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.explain: The 25% of the 36 students drawn evenly is more likely to represent the whole school than the 80% from the soccer field survey. But 36 students are not the whole school, so if another 36 students were drawn the result could be a little different, and you can't assert that it is exactly 25%.
y-m-18-07.s.s3.prompt: Design one survey method that better shows the thinking of the whole school. Write whom you will ask and how you will choose them.
y-m-18-07.s.s3.hint.0: Think about whether all 240 students have a chance of being chosen.
y-m-18-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how to divide so that people are not crowded in one grade or one place.
y-m-18-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it a method that gives people an equal (similar) chance of being chosen?
y-m-18-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Can you say how your method differs from Minseo's original method?
y-m-18-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about the number of people surveyed or the range too?
y-m-18-07.s.s3.model.0: From each class, I will draw 3 students by lottery of attendance numbers and ask them, so that I ask evenly in all the classes. If I ask in the classroom before class instead of during break, I won't meet only the students who gather on the field.
y-m-18-07.s.s3.model.1: I make a list for each grade and randomly draw the same 20 students from each grade and ask them. I want the thinking of every grade to be included.

y-m-18-08.title: How many cm will the sunflower be in the 8th week?
y-m-18-08.topic: Line graphs and predicting what comes next
y-m-18-08.goal: Predict what comes next from the pattern of change in a graph, know that a prediction has assumptions, and revise the prediction and degree of confidence after seeing new data.
y-m-18-08.material: The height of the sunflower in the classroom pot is measured on the same day every week and shown in a line graph. The height is in cm, and all values are taken to be measured exactly. The data is revealed one week at a time.
y-m-18-08.thinking.0: Predicting from the pattern of change in the data
y-m-18-08.thinking.1: Finding the assumption hidden in a prediction
y-m-18-08.thinking.2: Revising a prediction after seeing new data and information
y-m-18-08.prereq.1: Recognizing a change that grows steadily
y-m-18-08.s.s1.prompt: Each time data is revealed, choose how you predict the height in the 8th week.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write how much the height changed from the previous week for each week.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.hint.1: Write in one sentence what your prediction relies on assuming will continue.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.info: Week 1 is 5 cm, week 2 is 8 cm, week 3 is 11 cm, and week 4 is 14 cm. The points on the graph are almost on one line.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you predict the height in the 8th week?
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.after: It grew 3 cm every week for 4 weeks, so if the same speed continues, the 8th week is 5+3×7=26 cm. But the assumption that 'the same speed continues' is needed.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It will keep growing 3 cm every week and be about 26 cm
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You continued the pattern of change so far into the future for your prediction. It would be even better to be aware that there is an assumption that the pattern continues.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It will not grow any more and will be about 14 cm
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: There is not yet any clue in the data that the height stops.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: About 26 cm, but we have to watch whether the same speed continues
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You thought of the condition of the prediction along with the prediction.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.o.d: 4 weeks of data is too little to make any prediction
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: It is not that there is no clue at all. Growing steadily for 4 weeks is also information.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.info: Week 5 is 17 cm, week 6 is 19 cm, and week 7 is 20 cm. The amount grown is getting smaller: 3 cm, 2 cm, 1 cm.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now how do you predict the height in the 8th week?
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.after: The amount grown has shrunk as 3, 2, 1 cm, so the 8th week is likely to be near 20 cm. The first assumption of '3 cm every week' no longer fits the data.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Following the first pattern, it will still be about 26 cm
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You are holding on to the first pattern as it is. What if you combine the newly gathered data of weeks 5 to 7?
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It will be a value very close to 20 cm
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You revised your prediction to reflect the change of the last 3 weeks.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It will be shorter than in the 7th week
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: There is no evidence in the data that the height shrinks.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.o.d: See it as near 20 cm and measure the 8th week to check
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You said both the recent change and that we need to keep watching.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.info: The seed packet says, ‘This variety grows to a full height of about 20 cm.’ It was measured as 20 cm in week 8, 20 cm in week 9, and 20 cm in week 10.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: How do you now evaluate the first prediction of 26 cm from the first 4 weeks of data?
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.after: The pattern of the first 4 weeks fit well up to then. But the height did not keep growing at the same speed, and the new information of the variety's maximum height changed the assumption. When predicting what comes next, you should write down the assumption and revise it when new data arrives.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The method of predicting what comes next from a graph is itself useless
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: A wrong prediction does not make the method useless. Look at which assumption broke.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It sounded plausible at first, but the assumption of the same speed broke
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You pointed out what assumption the prediction rested on and how new information changed that assumption.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The first prediction was right and the value measured later is odd
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You tried to keep the first prediction while ignoring the later data and the seed packet's information.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The points of the first 4 weeks of data were not on one line
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The first data grew steadily. The problem is not the data but the assumption about the change to come.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.reflect: Was it reasonable for someone who had only the first 4 weeks of data to say the 8th week would be about 26 cm? What could you add to that statement so that it is less of a problem if it turns out wrong later?
y-m-18-08.s.s2.prompt: A friend who has only the first 4 weeks of data asks, “How many cm will it be in week 8?” Tell the friend your prediction together with its conditions.
y-m-18-08.s.s2.hint.0: First write how many cm it grew each week for 4 weeks, then continue to see how many cm it would be at which week if that continues.
y-m-18-08.s.s2.hint.1: Add one sentence that ends with ‘if ___.’
y-m-18-08.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. If it keeps ... like now, then ...
y-m-18-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the predicted value and the pattern it came from (e.g. 3 cm every week)?
y-m-18-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write at least one thing that, if it changes, could make it wrong?
y-m-18-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you suggest what to check in the future?
y-m-18-08.s.s2.model.0: If it keeps growing 3 cm every week like now, it will be about 26 cm in week 8. But there is no guarantee that it will keep growing at the same speed.
y-m-18-08.s.s2.model.1: It grew steadily up to week 4, so I predict about 26 cm. But if the growing speed changes it could be wrong, so let's measure every week and revise the prediction.
